topic: Lyle Bouck's 18-man platoon vs 700 paratroopers at Lanzerath, 1944
niche_fit: yes — documented Battle of the Bulge military history with concrete named soldiers and event
_transcript: On December 16, 1944, as dawn  broke over the Ardennes forest,   20-year-old Lieutenant Lyle Bouck  and his 18-man Intelligence and   Reconnaissance Platoon of the 394th Infantry  Regiment faced an overwhelming threat. For weeks, they had intercepted  German communications,   uncovering Hitler's plans to amass veteran  soldiers along the Belgium-Germany border. Now, Bouck's platoon faced the German Sixth  Panzer Army near the Belgian town of Lanzerath.   They were outnumbered and outgunned. Over  the radio, they received chilling news:   there would be no anti-tank  weapons, artillery support,   or any other help coming their way. Despite  this, the men prepared to defend a crucial road. At 5:30am, the Germans unleashed a  devastating 90-minute artillery barrage. For the next 20 hours, 18 men and  their 20-year-old would be all that   stood between 700 German Paratroopers and a  German victory at the Battle of The Bulge. At a mere 20 years old, Lyle Bouck had been  leading the Intelligence and Reconnaissance   Platoon of the 394th Infantry Regiment,  99th Infantry Division for about six months   by December 1944. His youth made him one of  the youngest officers in the American army. The platoon consisted of Bouck and his  17 men, all highly skilled marksmen   trained for specialized commando operations.  Despite not being trained for direct combat,   this elite unit undertook several perilous  missions deep behind enemy lines. On   their day-to-day operations, they infiltrated  German bases up to two miles beyond the front,   capturing unsuspecting Wehrmacht soldiers and  extracting valuable information from them,   sometimes through unconventional  means, all while evading detection. The group was also among the first to  be awarded the Combat Infantryman Badge,   a testament to their exceptional performance  on the battlefield during World War 2. Arriving in Le Havre alongside the 99th  Infantry Division in early November 1944,   they were deployed to the Ardennes  region by the end of the month,   taking over from the 60th  Regiment, 9th Infantry Division. By this time, despite the slow advance in  the dense Hürtgen Forest and the rugged   Vosges Mountains, a string of victories bred a  growing sense of confidence among Allied leaders,   with some even making the bold speculation  that the war might conclude before Christmas. But not within this platoon. As mid-December  1944 approached, the 99th Infantry Division's   Reconnaissance and Intelligence Platoon,  positioned close to the front lines,   sensed an impending storm brewing in the  Ardennes Forest. Under the leadership of Bouck,   this elite platoon had spent the preceding  weeks establishing communication listening   posts along the German-controlled Siegfried  Line, diligently gathering intelligence. What they uncovered was deeply troubling:   Hitler was amassing his most battle-hardened  veteran soldiers along the Belgium-Germany border,   preparing for a massive offensive that no one  believed possible at this late stage of the war. If successful, this maneuver would drive  a wedge between the British forces in the   north and the American forces in  the south, allowing the Germans to   methodically crush the Western armies and  put the Reich on top of the world again. Bouck was ready to do everything in  his power not to let that happen. Not long after their alarming discovery, Allied  command ordered Bouck and his men to take up   defensive positions on a ridge overlooking a  crucial road near the Belgian town of Lanzerath.  This time, instead of their usual  intelligence-gathering missions, Bouck's platoon   was tasked with digging into their position  and preparing to hold their ground at all costs   against the advancing German Sixth Panzer Army. The days of slipping behind enemy lines   unnoticed were over. Now, the platoon was  about to face a full-on German assault.  With no time to waste, especially as Commander  Bouck understood the strategic importance of   defending this Allied position on the road  to Losheim Gap, he ordered his men to begin   fortifying their bunkers immediately. The  20-year-old organized his men into two   9-man squads, supported by four forward artillery  observers – typically responsible for ranging in   howitzer fire, not engaging in direct combat. The men of the 394th found themselves in a   precarious position, lacking armor and  anti-tank capability after the assigned   Tank Destroyer company had departed without  notice. There was also no air support, backup,   or reinforcements. To make matters worse, Bouck  was informed via his only radio that the artillery   had "higher priority targets," leaving him  unable to rely on calling in a barrage.  Nonetheless, this tenacious platoon, led by their  fearless leader, stood ready to face the impending   storm and overwhelming odds head-on. Section Break  On December 15, 1944, Bouck ordered his men to  dig trenches overlooking the road to Lanzerath,   fortify them with pine logs, and set up  pillboxes with interlocking fields of fire.  With a forest at his back, an open field with  a barbed-wire fence separated Bouck's position   from the town. For his own protection,  the leader strategically placed his .30   caliber machine gun and two Browning Automatic  Rifles then traded one of the supply guys for   the .50 caliber machine gun in his jeep. As the night wore on, the distant clanking   of armor and the rumble of vehicles filled the  air. Bouck instructed his men to remain vigilant,   their eyes straining against the darkness. Despite their readiness, well-organized defenses,   and anticipation of a large-scale attack,  the sheer force of the German onslaught   was staggering when, at 5:30am, the Nazis  unleashed a powerful barrage of artillery.  The German plan was simple– to secure the road  to Lanzerath, allowing the 1st and 12th SS Panzer   Divisions to pass through. After the blistering  90-minute bombardment that shredded the trees   above Bouck's head, Wehrmacht infantry launched a  full-scale assault to breach American lines across   the Ardennes front, with the SS Panzers poised  to exploit the gap and make a dash for Antwerp. The task of securing Lanzerath Pass fell  to the 3rd Fallschirmjäger Division – a   unit of elite paratroopers that remained  in high morale despite being decimated back   in Normandy. Now bolstered by young boys and  older men previously deemed unfit for service,   the Division was still confident in  its ability to overcome the Americans.  Back atop Lanzerath ridge, Lyle Bouck and his  men gripped their rifles tightly as a battalion   of over 700 German Paratroopers marched  down the road towards the town, their boots   pounding against the frozen December earth. Bouck's voice was clear on his instructions:   to wait for the lead elements to pass,  then, only when the enemy was in range,   the Americans unleashed a hail of precise  gunfire, leaving the Germans scrambling for   cover in the nearby ditches as the machine  guns chewed up the ground around them.  Completely unaware of the opposition’s  numbers, the Paratroopers dispatched   a company of over 150 men to storm the  woods and eliminate the American threat.  As the Germans surged up the hill, their  fully automatic MP40 and MP44 submachine   guns chattering, the small group  of Americans remained steadfast,   cutting down the advancing enemy using fire from  their M1 Carbines and their heavy machine guns.  During the first attack, despite their undeniable  equipment and force superiority, not a single   German made it past the barbed-wire fence. Not on First Lieutenant Bouck’s watch. After a brief truce to allow German medics  to retrieve their wounded, the Paratroopers   launched a second assault, charging through  knee-deep snow under the cover of heavy mortar   and machine gun fire. The bitter cold bit at their  skin, but the adrenaline of battle and the hope   to win the war kept them pressing forward. Meanwhile, each of the 18 men of the I&R   Platoon fought with unwavering determination.  Private First Class Risto "Milo" Milosevich,   his feet bare and numb from the cold,  manned the .30-caliber machine gun alone,   as his socks were drying nearby when the Germans  arrived. Not far from him, his foxhole mate, in   a trance-like state, seamlessly switched between  his M1 rifle, a Grease Gun, and a Colt .45 pistol,   engaging the enemy with a fierce intensity. Behind the 700 paratroopers, the men of the   1st SS Panzer Corps found themselves mired in a  traffic jam, their timetable thrown into disarray   by the unexpected American resistance. The success  of the entire operation hinged on precise timing,   and they were already five hours behind schedule. Still determined to break through,   the 3rd Fallschirmjäger Division  launched another full-scale attack,   bolstered by the thundering support of  81-millimeter mortars and heavy artillery,   causing the ground to shake violently as massive  craters formed around the American foxholes. Despite the pressure from their much larger enemy,  Commander Bouck and his men continued to fight,   even as the Paratroopers drew close enough for  the Americans to see the whites of their eyes   as they engaged in hand-to-hand combat. By then, the battle at Lanzerath Ridge,   which had begun at 6:00am, now stretched  into its tenth hour. The Americans,   with their ammunition nearly spent  and several men nursing wounds,   clung to the hope of holding out just one more  hour to withdraw under the cover of darkness.  But they'd already achieved the unthinkable: for  almost a full day, eighteen American recon and   intelligence troops had single-handedly  delayed an entire German Panzer Army.  As dusk settled over the battlefield,  the Paratroopers launched their final,   desperate attack flanked through the forest,  triggering a series of tripwires attached   to grenades instead of attacking head-on, the  resulting explosions echoing through the trees.  This time, while the Americans attempted  to adjust their positions, with their   ammunition exhausted and their defenses  breached, realizing the fight was over,   they surrendered and were quickly taken prisoner. Against all odds, and despite three large attacks,   not a single American life was lost in the  epic stand at Lanzerath Ridge. In contrast,   the commando force had wounded  or taken the lives of 92 enemies.  That day, the Americans had fought with  such tenacity and skill that the Germans   couldn't believe a mere 18 men had defended  the woods. Despite the forest being clear   following the surrender, the advancing  division hesitated to advance until   the commanding officer of the 1st SS Panzer  Division, Joachim Peiper, arrived at 1:00am.  Peiper then personally led a  battalion of paratroopers into   the forest to verify it was empty. The delay, caused by heavy traffic,   destroyed bridges, and the determined defense by  Bouck's platoon, had far-reaching consequences.  Instead of reaching the Meuse River on the  first day, as planned, the Germans made   little progress. The entire northern wing  of the attack, a crucial part of Hitler's   surprise offensive through the Ardennes, fell  hopelessly behind schedule and never recovered. Following his capture, Bouck, who was  still unaware of the impact his platoon   had in the entire battle, was consumed  by a sense of failure, the weight of the   battle bearing down on his young shoulders. As the clock struck midnight on December   17, First Lieutenant Lyle Bouck turned 21  years old. The Intelligence and Reconnaissance   Platoon was then sent on a grueling 11-day  train ride to a prison camp in Germany,   where they endured four months in a freezing  outdoor camp during the harsh German winter.  Bouck was about to succumb  to hypothermia, starvation,   and dehydration when his old unit – the 99th  Division – finally marched in and rescued him.  The heroic actions of this platoon  went largely unnoticed until 1965,   when an Army publication regarding the Battle of  the Bulge briefly mentioned them. This spurred   one of Bouck's men to reach out and encourage  him to seek recognition for their efforts.  Bouck contacted his former division  commander, Major General Walter E. Lauer,   who nominated him for the Silver Star. However,  the rest of the platoon was still not recognized.  Driven by a desire to honor his men, Bouck  tirelessly lobbied the government until,   on October 25, 1981, a World War 2 Valor Awards  Ceremony, the Intelligence and Reconnaissance   Platoon of the 394th Infantry Regiment, 99th  Infantry Division received the Presidential   Unit Citation, a long-overdue recognition.  Additionally, five members were awarded the   Distinguished Service Cross, four received  Silver Stars, and 10 Bronze Stars with Valor   were bestowed, cementing the platoon's status  as one of the most decorated in World War 2.  The fierce resistance of Bouck's platoon played  a pivotal role in stalling the German advance,   forever altering the course of the Battle of the  Bulge. As author Alex Kershaw stated: [QUOTE]  "Had they not stood and held the Germans  and halted their attack, or rather postponed   it for a crucial 24 hours, the Battle of the  Bulge would have been a great German victory."
